water-evaporation.title: Evaporation: water molecules leave the surface

text.general: Water molecules that move fast enough escape from a wet surface into the air. Plants release water too.
text.expert: Molecules at a wet surface that move fast enough escape into the air as vapor. Evapotranspiration also includes water released by plants.

water-evaporation.value: A larger flux shows more molecules leaving the liquid.

water-vapor.title: Water vapor: single molecules in the air

text.general: Water vapor is an invisible gas of separate water molecules. Where air cools enough, they gather into cloud droplets.
text.expert: Water vapor is an invisible gas of separate H₂O molecules. Where air cools enough, vapor condenses onto small particles and forms cloud droplets.

water-vapor.value: A larger column amount shows more molecules in the air.

water-precipitation.title: Precipitation: droplets grow and fall

text.general: Cloud droplets that grow large enough fall as rain. One raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets' worth of water.
text.expert: Cloud droplets that grow large enough fall as rain. A typical cloud droplet is about 10 µm in radius and a typical raindrop about 1 mm, so a raindrop holds roughly a million cloud droplets' worth of water.

water-precipitation.value: A higher rate shows drops falling more often.

no2-photolysis.title: NO₂ and sunlight make ozone near the ground

text.general: Sunlight splits NO₂ and frees an oxygen atom. That atom joins an oxygen molecule (O₂) to form ozone (O₃).
text.expert: Sunlight at wavelengths shorter than roughly 400 nm splits NO₂. The freed oxygen atom joins an O₂ molecule to form ozone; M is any air molecule that carries away the extra energy (drawn as N₂).

no2-photolysis.value: A larger NO₂ column shows more NO₂ molecules taking part.

ozone-chapman.title: How ozone forms in the stratosphere

text.general: Ultraviolet light splits oxygen molecules (O₂) into single atoms. Each atom joins another O₂ to form ozone (O₃).
text.expert: Ultraviolet light at wavelengths shorter than about 242 nm splits O₂. Each oxygen atom joins another O₂ to form ozone (first steps of the Chapman mechanism); M is any air molecule, drawn as N₂. Total ozone counts the whole column, most of it in the stratosphere.

ozone-chapman.value: A larger ozone column shows more ozone being formed.

thermal-air.title: Temperature is how fast molecules move

text.general: Air temperature measures how fast air molecules move on average. Warmer air means faster molecules.
text.expert: Air temperature measures the average kinetic energy of its molecules, mostly N₂ and O₂. Their typical speed grows with the square root of the absolute temperature.

thermal-air.value: Molecule speed in this view follows √T for the selected month, so the change between months is real but small.

thermal-surface.title: Temperature is how fast particles move

text.general: Land surface temperature is the temperature of the ground itself. This view uses air molecules to show the same idea: hotter means faster random motion.
text.expert: Land surface temperature is the temperature of the ground itself, where atoms vibrate in place rather than fly freely. The view shows air molecules at that temperature to illustrate the same idea: hotter means faster random motion.

thermal-surface.value: Molecule speed in this view follows √T for the selected month, so the change between months is real but small.

aerosol-scale.title: Aerosols are particles, not molecules

text.general: Aerosols are tiny solid or liquid particles such as dust, smoke and sea salt. Even a small one is hundreds of times wider than a gas molecule.
text.expert: Aerosols are solid or liquid particles such as dust, smoke and sea salt, from a few nanometers to tens of micrometers across. Even a small 100 nm particle is hundreds of times wider than a gas molecule (about 0.3 nm). The UV aerosol index is a unitless measure that responds mainly to UV-absorbing aerosols such as dust and smoke.

aerosol-scale.value: A higher index shows more grains.

photosynthesis.title: Green leaves: photosynthesis

text.general: Leaves use light to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, and release oxygen. NDVI measures how green the land looks from space.
text.expert: Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts of leaf cells absorbs light and uses it to build sugar from CO₂ and water, releasing O₂. NDVI measures how green the surface looks from space: (NIR − red) / (NIR + red).

photosynthesis.value: A higher NDVI shows more molecules being exchanged.

soil-pores.title: Soil moisture: water between soil grains

text.general: Soil is grains with gaps between them. Soil moisture is the water held in those gaps, here in the top 10 cm.
text.expert: Soil is grains with gaps (pores) between them. Soil moisture is the water held in those pores; here it is the water in the top 10 cm, in kilograms per square meter.

soil-pores.value: A wetter month shows more of the pore space filled with water.
